docs.title: Geometry update note
docs.text:
Shell workflows do not keep a persistent geometry lock state. Geometry-changing updates are applied to the config directly, and the next preview or run rebuilds from the updated JSON.

See CLI Usage for full shell command reference, including explore.

docs.title: Connect an external agent through MCP
docs.text:
Build/install the native project following the installation guide, then install the required extras from the same checkout:

python -m pip install '.[mcp,cad,results,visualization]'
sphinxsim capabilities --json

Configure an MCP client with the installed native CLI, for example:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sphinxsim": {
      "command": "/path/to/venv/bin/sphinxsim",
      "args": ["mcp", "--root", "/workspace"]
    }
  }
}

The server uses the official SDK and stdio transport. It requires no product account, cloud gateway or proprietary handshake. The process owner selects the workspace and supplies resource isolation. Do not expose unrestricted workspaces.

Discover the running inventory instead of copying a stale schema. capabilities reports source evidence and limitations; compile returns a new configuration; validate checks an explicit config_file; project_inspect returns the resource inventory; submit requires that reviewed project inventory. Use submission_id for retries. geometry defaults to a persistent CAD job. All job operations take the returned complete reference object, including its request hash.

A native desktop is optional. Start it with sphinxsim desktop serve ... and give its owner-only reference file to sphinxsim mcp --root ... --desktop-reference .... Only then is desktop advertised. Observe status, then send the explicit instance/version and operation scope; the server never silently fetches a fresh version to make a stale edit succeed. Remote computer-use drivers are external.

Verified artifacts use sphinxsim://jobs/{job_id}/artifacts/{name} resources. Reads are limited to published files and 1 MiB per resource; use owner-provided file delivery for large assets. Resource access rechecks published size/hash evidence.

Read the native workflow guide for CLI examples, JSON contracts, execution lifecycle, quality interpretation and test boundaries.

The Agent and Chatbot use this same stdio service through the official MCP SDK. Tool discovery includes the following authoring and analysis operations.

Operation Input and result config_generate Generate validated native JSON into an explicit workspace file config_update Update and validate a selected configuration before saving config_propose Return a validated draft proposal and admission report case_prepare Copy a configuration and stage its STL/data resources set_friction_angle Update one plastic-continuum body using degrees analyze_result Evaluate a runout or declarative analysis plan compare_results Compare completed measurements with a target results_render Render a PNG from verified published geometry and particles

These tools use the same snake_case names, JSON Schema input validation, structured object results, workspace paths, and MCP error responses as the native operations. submit and the job operations support Windows and POSIX. Generated case resources are copied into content-addressed files under the working project. Result analysis checks the job's complete reference, frozen input inventory, and published asset hashes before reading particle data.

When launched by Workbench, its connection enables a workbench tool for draft status, revision-bound proposals, and workflow observation. Discover this tool from the running server. Apply and save proposals through the desktop editor. The Chatbot accepts /mcp <tool> <JSON arguments> for explicit calls, including with a mock provider. For example, /mcp capabilities {} queries the native inventory. Real LLM providers also select discovered tools through structured requests and receive the actual operation results before answering.

The optional skill guides experimental decisions; install it through your client's supported skill mechanism. It grants no access.

No Docker image is required by this protocol. Image names, GPU devices, remote desktop servers, browser embedding and authentication are deployment choices outside this repository's agent implementation.

docs.title: Total Lagrangian Formulation for Solid Mechanics
docs.text:
Considering continuum mechanics in the total Lagrangian framework, the kinematics and dynamic equations are expressed in terms of the initial, undeformed reference configuration \(\Omega^0 \subset oldsymbol{R}^d\) with \(d\) denoting the dimension. A deformation map \(\varphi\) between the initial configuration \(\Omega^0\) and current deformed configuration \(\Omega = \varphi \left( \Omega^0 ight)\) describes the body deformation at time \(t\) as

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{r} = \varphi \left( oldsymbol{r}^0, t ight), \label{deformation-map} \end{equation}\]

where \( oldsymbol{r}^0\) and \( oldsymbol{r}\) are the initial and current positions of a material point, respectively. Subsequently, the deformation gradient tensor \( oldsymbol{F}\) is given by

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{F} = abla^0 oldsymbol{r} = abla^0 oldsymbol{u} + oldsymbol{I}, \label{deformation-gradient} \end{equation}\]

where \( oldsymbol{u} = oldsymbol{r} - oldsymbol{r}^0\) is the displacement, \( abla^0 \equiv rac{\partial}{\partial oldsymbol{r}^0}\) the gradient operator with respect to the initial configuration \(\Omega^0\) and $ oldsymbol{I} $ the identity matrix.

The conservation equations for mass and momentum in the total Lagrangian formulation can be expressed as

\[ egin{equation} egin{cases} ho = J^{-1} ho^0 \ ho^0 \ddot { oldsymbol{u}} = abla^0 \cdot oldsymbol{P}^{\operatorname{T}}, \end{cases} \label{conservation-equations} \end{equation}\]

where \( ho^0\) and \( ho\) are the initial and current densities, respectively, \(J = \det( oldsymbol{F})\), \(\ddot { oldsymbol{u}}\) the acceleration, \( oldsymbol{P}\) the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor, and \(\operatorname{T}\) the matrix transposition operator. While \( oldsymbol{P}\) can be obtained directly by

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{P} = oldsymbol{F} oldsymbol{S}, \label{piola-stress} \end{equation}\]

where \( oldsymbol{S}\) is the second Piola-Kirchhoff stress tensor, \( oldsymbol{P}\) is obtained by the alternative Kirchhoff-stress approach in this work as

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{P} = oldsymbol{ au} oldsymbol{F}^{-\operatorname{T}}. \label{kirchhoff-stress} \end{equation}\]

Here, the Kirchhoff stress \( oldsymbol{ au}\) is decomposed into volumetric and deviatoric components, and can be derived form the following strain energy function \cite{simo2006computational}

\[ egin{equation} \mathfrak{W}_e = \mathfrak{W}_v \left( J ight) + \mathfrak{W}_s \left( ar { oldsymbol{b}} ight). \label{strain-energy} \end{equation}\]

Here, the volume-preserving left Cauchy-Green deformation gradient tensor \( ar { oldsymbol{b}} = J^ {- rac{2}{d}} oldsymbol{b} = \left| oldsymbol{b} ight|^{ - rac{1}{d}} oldsymbol{b}\) with \( oldsymbol{b} = oldsymbol{F} oldsymbol{F}^{\operatorname{T}}\). For neo-Hookean materials, the volume-dependent strain energy \(\mathfrak{W}_v \left( J ight)\) weighted by the bulk modulus \(K\) can be expressed as

\[ egin{equation} \mathfrak{W}_v \left( J ight) = rac{1}{2}K\left[ rac{1}{2}\left( J^2 - 1 ight) - \ln J ight], \label{volumetric-energy} \end{equation}\]

whereas the shear-dependent strain energy \(\mathfrak{W}_s \left( ar { oldsymbol{b}} ight)\) weighted by the shear modulus \(G\) \cite{yue2015continuum} is given by

\[ egin{equation} \mathfrak{W}_s \left( ar{ oldsymbol{b}} ight) = rac{1}{2} G \left( \operatorname{tr} \left( ar { oldsymbol{b}} ight) - d ight). \label{deviatoric-energy} \end{equation}\]

Then, the Kirchhoff stress tensor \( oldsymbol{ au}\) can be derived as

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{ au} = rac{\partial \mathfrak{W}_e}{\partial oldsymbol{F} } oldsymbol{F}^{\operatorname{T}} = rac{K}{2}\left( J^2 - 1 ight) oldsymbol{I} + G \operatorname{dev} \left( ar { oldsymbol{b}} ight), \label{Kirchhoff_stress} \end{equation}\]

where egin{equation} \operatorname{dev} \left( ar{ oldsymbol{b}} ight) = ar { oldsymbol{b}} - rac{1}{d} \operatorname{tr} \left( ar{ oldsymbol{b}} ight) \mathbb{I} = J^ {- rac{2}{d}} \left[ oldsymbol{b} - rac{1}{d} \operatorname{tr} \left( oldsymbol{b} ight) \mathbb{I} ight]. \label{deviatoric-stress} \end{equation}

The deviatoric operator \(\operatorname{dev}\left( ar{ oldsymbol{b}} ight)\) returns the trace-free part of \( ar{ oldsymbol{b}}\), i.e., \(\operatorname{tr} \left( \operatorname{dev}\left( ar{ oldsymbol{b}} ight) ight)\) is equal to zero. Note that while the volumetric component of the constitutive Eq. \(\eqref{Kirchhoff_stress}\) can be modified depending on the material property and all counterparts are appropriate for this study, only the Eq. \(\eqref{Kirchhoff_stress}\) is utilized in this study.

docs.title: Update Lagrangian Formulation for Solid Mechanics
docs.text:
The update Lagrangian formulation is an alternative approach to the total Lagrangian formulation. In this framework, the kinematics and dynamic equations are expressed in terms of the current, deformed configuration \(\Omega \subset oldsymbol{R}^d\). So the governing equations are very similar to those of fluid mechanics in Lagrangian framework. Let \( ho\) denote the current mass density, \(\mathbf{v}\) the velocity vector, \(\mathbf{g}\) the body force per unit mass, and \( oldsymbol{\sigma}\) the Cauchy stress tensor. In the absence of thermal coupling, the local balance equations for mass and linear momentum are written as \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}

\[ egin{equation} rac{D ho}{Dt} + ho abla\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0, \label{eq:density} \end{equation}\]

and

\[ egin{equation} ho rac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt} = abla\cdot oldsymbol{\sigma} + ho\mathbf{g}. \label{eq:moementum} \end{equation}\]

Here, the Cauchy stress is decomposed into a deviatoric contribution and a hydrostatic contribution,

\[ egin{equation} oldsymbol{\sigma} = \mathbf{s} - p\mathbf{I}, \label{eq:CoxPnull} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{s}\) denotes the deviatoric stress tensor, \(p\) is the pressure according to the sign convention adopted in fluid mechanics, and \(\mathbf{I}\) is the second-order identity tensor. Consequently,

\[ \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{s})=0, \]

and the mean or hydrostatic stress becomes

\[ egin{equation} \sigma_H = rac{1}{d}\operatorname{tr}( oldsymbol{\sigma}) = -p. \label{eq:hydrostatic} \end{equation}\]

This decomposition is particularly important for the present constitutive framework. Plastic yielding is governed only by the deviatoric stress through the \(J_2\) criterion, whereas the hydrostatic stress does not influence yielding directly \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}. In contrast, hydrostatic stress plays an essential role in ductile damage because it promotes the growth of microscopic voids and defects and therefore enters the adopted damage formulation through stress triaxiality \cite{Kachanov1986,LemaitreChaboche2004,CaleyronEtAl2012}.

The velocity gradient is defined as

\[ egin{equation} \mathbf{L} = abla\mathbf{v}, \label{eq:velocity-gradient} \end{equation}\]

and is decomposed into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts,

\[ egin{equation} \mathbf{D} = rac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{L}+\mathbf{L}^{T} ight), \qquad \mathbf{W} = rac{1}{2} \left( \mathbf{L}-\mathbf{L}^{T} ight), \label{eq:velocity-gradient-decomposition} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{D}\) is the rate-of-deformation tensor and \(\mathbf{W}\) is the spin tensor. The deviatoric part of the rate-of-deformation tensor is

\[ egin{equation} \mathbf{D}' = \mathbf{D} - rac{1}{d} \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{D})\mathbf{I}, \label{eq:deviatoric-rate-of-deformation} \end{equation}\]

where \(d\) denotes the spatial dimension.

Since metal cutting involves large deformation and significant material rotation, an objective stress update is required. The updated-Lagrangian solid formulation employed in the underlying SPH framework uses a corotational stress update for the deviatoric stress \cite{ZhangEtAl2025}. In the elastic regime, the deviatoric stress rate is expressed as

\[ egin{equation} \dot{\mathbf{s}} = 2G\mathbf{D}' + \mathbf{s}\mathbf{W}^{T} + \mathbf{W}\mathbf{s}, \label{eq:corotational-stress-update} \end{equation}\]

where

\[ egin{equation} G = rac{E}{2(1+ u)} \label{eq:shear-modulus} \end{equation}\]

is the shear modulus, \(E\) is Young's modulus, and \( u\) is Poisson's ratio. The corresponding bulk modulus is

\[ egin{equation} K = rac{E}{3(1-2 u)}. \label{eq:bulk-modulus} \end{equation}\]

These relations form the elastic part of the constitutive update employed by the J2 material model. They are consistent with the continuum-mechanics formulation of elastoplastic solids \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006} and with the updated-Lagrangian SPH solid-dynamics formulation developed by Zhang et al.~\cite{ZhangEtAl2025}.

docs.title: J2 Plasticity
docs.text:
The popular elastic-plastic nonlinear material model, often used for metal, is the isotropic \(J_2\) plasticity with linear isotropic hardening. The \(J_2\), or von Mises, model is widely used for ductile metallic materials because plastic yielding is assumed to depend primarily on distortional deformation rather than on hydrostatic pressure \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}.

The second invariant of the deviatoric stress tensor is defined as

\[\begin{equation} J_2 = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{s}:\mathbf{s}. \label{eq:second-invariant} \end{equation}\]

The corresponding von Mises equivalent stress is

\[\begin{equation} \sigma_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sqrt{3J_2} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{s}:\mathbf{s}}. \label{eq:von-mises-stress} \end{equation}\]

In conventional notation, the yield function may therefore be written as

\[\begin{equation} \Phi = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}f = \sigma_{\mathrm{eq}} - \sigma_f, \label{eq:yield-function} \end{equation}\]

where the current flow stress for linear isotropic hardening is

\[\begin{equation} \sigma_f = \sigma_y + H\alpha. \label{eq:flow-stress} \end{equation}\]

Here, \(\sigma_y\) denotes the initial yield stress, \(H\) is the isotropic hardening modulus, and \(\alpha\) is the accumulated hardening variable \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}.

When

\[ f\leq0, \]

the stress state is elastically admissible. When

\[ f>0, \]

the trial stress lies outside the expanded yield surface and a plastic correction is required.

An important feature of J2 plasticity is that the yield criterion does not depend on hydrostatic stress \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}. Consequently, two material points with identical deviatoric stress but different mean stresses reach yielding at the same value of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{eq}}\). This assumption is appropriate for describing plastic flow in dense ductile metals. However, it is insufficient for describing ductile fracture because the nucleation and growth of cavities are strongly affected by hydrostatic stress \cite{Kachanov1986,LemaitreChaboche2004,CaleyronEtAl2012}.

The present formulation therefore separates the two physical mechanisms: J2 plasticity governs irreversible plastic flow, whereas the damage model introduces hydrostatic-stress sensitivity into the failure process. This separation allows the existing J2 constitutive model to be retained while extending the formulation toward ductile fracture.

docs.title: Equivalent Plastic Strain and Hardening
docs.text:
The tensorial plastic deformation generated by the J2 model is represented by a scalar accumulated equivalent plastic strain, \(\bar{\varepsilon}^{p}\), which provides a convenient history variable for isotropic hardening and ductile damage \cite{Borja2013,SimoHughes2006}.

For associative J2 plasticity, the equivalent plastic strain rate is conventionally defined as

\[\begin{equation} \dot{\bar{\varepsilon}}^{p} = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{3} \dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{p} : \dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^{p} }, \label{eq:equivalent-plastic-strain-rate} \end{equation}\]

or, in incremental form,

\[\begin{equation} \Delta\bar{\varepsilon}^{p} = \sqrt{ \frac{2}{3} \Delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p} : \Delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{p} }. \label{eq:incremental-equivalent-plastic-strain} \end{equation}\]

In the present implementation, the J2 plasticity model already contains an evolving scalar state variable named HardeningFactor}. This variable is used as the accumulated plastic-history measure,

\[\begin{equation} \alpha \equiv \bar{\varepsilon}^{p}. \label{eq:plastic-history-measure} \end{equation}\]

The current yield stress consequently evolves according to

\[\begin{equation} \sigma_f = \sigma_y + H\bar{\varepsilon}^{p}. \label{eq:current-yield-stress} \end{equation}\]

This identification is particularly advantageous for the damage extension introduced in this work. No independent plastic-history variable needs to be introduced specifically for the damage model. Instead, the accumulated equivalent plastic strain generated by the existing J2 algorithm is directly reused as the principal history variable governing damage initiation and damage evolution. This provides a natural connection between the original J2 constitutive formulation \cite{ZhangEtAl2025} and the ductile damage formulation of Caleyron et al.~\cite{CaleyronEtAl2012}.

For a plastic trial state, the scalar plastic correction used in the current implementation is related to the excess of the trial yield function. The corresponding correction measure is

\[\begin{equation} \Delta\lambda = \frac{1}{2} \frac{f_{\mathrm{trial}}} {G+H/3}, \qquad f_{\mathrm{trial}}>0, \label{eq:CoxPnull} \end{equation}\]

from which the equivalent plastic-strain increment can be expressed as

\[\begin{equation} \Delta\bar{\varepsilon}^{p} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \Delta\lambda. \label{eq:CoxPnull} \end{equation}\]

The accumulated plastic strain is then updated according to

\[\begin{equation} \bar{\varepsilon}^{p}_{n+1} = \bar{\varepsilon}^{p}_{n} + \Delta\bar{\varepsilon}^{p}. \label{eq:CoxPnull} \end{equation}\]

Because

\[ \Delta\bar{\varepsilon}^{p}\geq0, \]

the equivalent plastic strain is an irreversible history variable.

This relationship establishes the first direct connection between plasticity and damage in the present model:

\[\begin{equation} \boxed{ J_2\ \text{plastic flow} \longrightarrow \Delta\bar{\varepsilon}^{p} \longrightarrow \bar{\varepsilon}^{p} \longrightarrow \text{damage evolution} } \label{eq:CoxPnull} \end{equation}\]

Thus, damage is not driven by an independently prescribed geometric separation criterion. Instead, it develops from the accumulated irreversible plastic deformation already calculated by the underlying J2 constitutive model. This concept is consistent with continuum ductile-damage formulations in which plastic strain acts as an internal driving variable for the accumulation of material defects \cite{Kachanov1986,LemaitreChaboche2004,CaleyronEtAl2012}.

docs.title: Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH)
docs.text: SPH is a meshless Lagrangian particle method that was originally developed for astrophysical problems by Lucy \cite{lucy1977numerical} and Gingold and Monaghan \cite{gingold1977smoothed}. In SPHinXsys, the SPH method is employed to solve the governing equations of fluid and solid mechanics, as well as their interactions.

docs.title: Gradient Approximation
docs.text:
In SPH discretization of the partial differential equation of fluid dynamics, the kernel approximation for the gradient operator acting on a smooth field \(\psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}} ight)\)

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi\left( oldsymbol{ m r} ight)\approx \int_{\Omega} abla\psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}} ight) W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{v*}, h ight)d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}= -\int_{\Omega}\psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}} ight) abla W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{*},h ight) d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}. \label{SPHapproximation} \end{equation}\]

where \(W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}, h ight)\) is the kernel function scaled by the smoothing length \(h\). While the first stage introduces smoothing errors by the kernel function, the second stage entails integration by parts, assuming the kernel function vanishes at the boundary of a compact support. Through Taylor expansion, for Eq. \(\eqref{SPHapproximation}\) one can find that the zero-order consistency condition is

\[ egin{equation} \int_{\Omega} abla W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{*},h ight)d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}=0, \label{zeroorderkernel} \end{equation}\]

and the first-order consistency condition is

\[ egin{equation} -\int_{\Omega}\left( oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}- oldsymbol{ m r} ight)\otimes abla W \left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}, h ight)d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}=\mathbf{I}. \label{firstorderconsistencyintegration} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{I}\) represents the identity matrix. Zero-order consistency condition allows rewriting the kernel approximation in two equivalent forms:

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi\left( oldsymbol{ m r} ight)= \int_{\Omega}\left(\psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}} ight) - \psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}} ight) ight) abla W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}, h ight)d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*} \ \equiv -\int_{\Omega}\left(\psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}} ight) + \psi\left({ oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}} ight) ight) abla W\left( oldsymbol{ m r}- oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}, h ight)d oldsymbol{ m r}^{*}. \label{SPHgradientapproximations} \end{equation}\]

By introducing particle summation, the first approximation in Eq. \(\eqref{SPHgradientapproximations}\) can be further approximated for an SPH particle \(i\) as

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi_{i} = \sum_{j} \psi_{ij} abla W_{ij}V_{j}. \label{strong} \end{equation}\]

where \(V_{j}\) is the volume of the neighbor particles within the support, and the particle-pair difference is \(\psi_{ij}= \psi_{i}-\psi_{j}\). This form is often referred to as a symmetric or non-conservative form. Similarly, the second approximation in Eq. \(\eqref{SPHgradientapproximations}\) can be also approximated as

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi_{i} = -\sum_{j} \left(\psi_{i}+\psi_{j} ight) abla W_{ij}V_{j}. \label{weak} \end{equation}\]

where the particle-pair sum is employed. This form, known as the anti-symmetric or conservative form, ensures discrete conservation and is commonly chosen in classical SPH methods for discretizing physical conservation laws.

For the non-conservative form of Eq. \(\eqref{strong}\), zero-order consistency is automatically satisfied as the particle-pair difference is used. To achieve first-order consistency, one requires that the approximation of Eq. \(\eqref{firstorderconsistencyintegration}\) satisfies

\[ egin{equation} -\sum_{j} oldsymbol{ m r}_{ij}\otimes abla W_{ij}V_{j} = \mathbf{I}. \label{firstorderconsistency} \end{equation}\]

To precisely fulfill the above condition, the KGC approach \cite{randles1996smoothed}, introducing a correction matrix \(\mathbf{B}_{i}\) to adjust the gradient of the kernel function, can be employed, so that one has

\[ egin{equation} -\sum_{j} oldsymbol{ m r}_{ij}\otimes \mathbf{B}_{i} abla W_{ij}V_{j}=\mathbf{I}, \quad \mathbf{B}_{i}=\left(-\sum_{j} \mathbf{r}_{ij}\otimes abla W_{ij}V_{j} ight)^{-1}. \label{KGC} \end{equation}\]

With the KGC, Eq. \(\eqref{strong}\) is modified as

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi_{i} = \sum_{j} \psi_{ij} \mathbf{B}_{i} abla W_{ij}V_{j}. \label{strong-corrected} \end{equation}\]

Note that, introducing \(\mathbf{B}_{i}\) does not affect the zero-order consistency of Eq. \(\eqref{strong-corrected}\). Also note that, although the non-conservation form is not desirable for the discretization of physical conservation laws, Eq. \(\eqref{strong-corrected}\) is often used when the conservation is not a primary concern because it can reproduce the linear gradient and achieve second-order accuracy.

In the conservative form of Eq. \(\eqref{weak}\), where the particle-pair sum other than the difference is used, the zero-order consistency condition becomes nontrivial as

\[ egin{equation} \sum_{j} abla W_{ij}V_{j}=0. \label{zeroorderconsistency} \end{equation}\]

Litvinov et al. \cite{litvinov2015towards} proposed a particle relaxation process driven by a constant background pressure assuming invariant particle volume. After the particles are settled down or fully relaxed, Eq. \(\eqref{zeroorderconsistency}\) is satisfied for the zero-order consistency. To achieve first-order constancy, as a straightforward extension for Eq. \(\eqref{weak}\), one may suggest

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi_{i}=-\sum_{j} \left(\psi_{i}\mathbf{B'}_{i}+\psi_{j}\mathbf{B'}_{j} ight) abla W_{ij}V_{j}. \label{weak-corrected} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{B'}_{i}\) and \(\mathbf{B'}_{j}\) are some correction matrices for particles \(i\) and \(j\), is able to reproduce a linear gradient similar to Eq. \(\eqref{strong-corrected}\). How to obtain these correction matrices is not straightforward, and various attempts based on the original KGC matrix for the non-conservative form have been carried out. One widely used formulation, introduced by Oger et al. \cite{oger2007improved}, is expressed as,

\[ egin{equation} abla\psi_{i}=-\sum_{j} \left(\psi_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}+\psi_{j}\mathbf{B}_{j} ight) abla W_{ij}V_{j}. \label{Oger-corrected} \end{equation}\]

where the KGC matrix is applied for each particle pair separately.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: SPHinXsim includes a pre-run configuration visualizer that renders your simulation setup — geometries, bodies, boundary conditions, and physics annotations — before the expensive C++ solver starts. This lets you catch setup mistakes early and build an intuitive picture of what the simulation will run.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
PyVista is required:

pip install sphinxsim[visualization]

For responsive persistent preview in interactive shell mode, install pyvistaqt with a Qt binding backend:

pip install pyvistaqt PySide6
# alternatively: pip install pyvistaqt PyQt5

The compiled C++ extension (_sphinxsys_core_2d or _sphinxsys_core_3d) is required for preview geometry generation. The preview always attempts to build VTP meshes first and automatically falls back to cached shape bounds when VTP files are not produced. If neither source can provide a configured shape, the preview stops with an error instead of opening an empty scene. Rebuild or update the SPHinXsim Python binding library if the native geometry is missing; rebuilding only the C++ projects may leave the Python binding out of date.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Element Visual style Colour Fluid body shapes Solid surface Blue Solid body shapes Solid surface Grey Continuum body shapes Solid surface Amber Other defined shapes Wireframe Green Inlet/Outlet oriented boxes Wireframe Red Constraint region oriented boxes Wireframe Yellow System domain bounding box Wireframe White (10 % opacity) Generated particles (--with-particles) Points White (per-body colour)

Each shape and oriented box is labelled with an annotation that includes:

  • Body shapes: material type, density, sound speed, thermal boundary type (when applicable).
  • Oriented boxes: BC type (emitter, bi-directional), inflow speed or pressure, and particle-relaxation constraints targeting that oriented box.
  • Gravity: shown in the lower-left corner when a gravity vector is defined.

In an interactive preview window with the JSON editor open, hovering an annotation enlarges it. Clicking an annotation reveals and selects its corresponding configuration entry in the editor; this expands the entry's ancestors and clears the editor filter if needed to make the entry visible.

docs.title: Basic preview (direct command)
docs.text:
sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json

This opens an interactive PyVista window showing the geometry. The original JSON file is passed directly to the C++ SPHSimulation — it is the single source of truth, no intermediate copy is written.

docs.title: Preview with generated particles
docs.text:
sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json --with-particles

Also runs particle generation (generateParticles()) and overlays the latest generated particle cloud for each particle-generation body. This is opt-in because particle generation can be expensive.

When particles are shown:

  • Regular body shapes are hidden to keep the view clear.
  • Oriented boxes, constraints, observers, gravity, and all annotations remain visible.
  • One particle cloud is rendered per body, using the highest step VTP file (BodyName_<step>.vtp or BodyName_ite_<step>.vtp).
  • A small label shows the body name and step number for each particle cloud.

This is useful for verifying particle distribution and spacing before running the full simulation.

docs.title: Off-screen rendering
docs.text:
sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json --off-screen

Renders to an off-screen buffer instead of opening a window. Intended for automated testing or headless environments.

docs.title: Screenshot output
docs.text:
sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json --screenshot preview.png
# or equivalently:
sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json -s preview.png

Saves a screenshot of the preview to the specified file instead of opening an interactive window. This automatically enables off-screen rendering, so --off-screen is implied and does not need to be passed separately.

Supported formats depend on your PyVista/VTK build, but typically include PNG, JPEG, and TIFF.

sphinxsim preview path/to/config.json -s preview.png
📸 Screenshot saved to: preview.png

This is useful for: - Generating preview images for reports or documentation. - Batch-generating previews in CI pipelines. - Headless environments where no display is available.

docs.title: Interactive shell
docs.text:
preview is available as a first-class shell command:

In shell mode, preview keeps a persistent window and returns control to the shell prompt. Running preview again updates the existing window and rebuilds geometry from the current config.

Notes: - preview --screenshot ... is one-shot and does not use the persistent window. - Persistent interactive mode relies on pyvistaqt plus a Qt backend (for example PySide6 or PyQt5). - In the Qt-backed persistent window, the full-height dark configuration editor on the right presents JSON fields as a searchable property tree: setting names on the left and editable value boxes on the right. It uses type-appropriate controls for booleans, numbers, and common enumerations. Click the Setting ▾ column header to open the editor menu with Expand, Collapse, Revert, and Reload. To modify a list, right-click its row and choose Add, or right-click an entry to Duplicate, Remove, or Move up/Move down. Only actions available for that row are highlighted; unavailable actions are dimmed. A change is saved only when you press Ctrl+S; it validates and atomically saves the currently loaded JSON file before rebuilding the preview. Running preview asks for confirmation before discarding unapplied editor changes. Loading a different configuration and running preview rebinds the editor to that file. If the persistent Preview window is closed, running preview again creates a fresh window and reattaches the editor.

sphinxsim> load config.json
✅ Loaded config from config.json

sphinxsim> preview
🖼  Building configuration preview for: .../config.json
   Building C++ geometry; bounds cache fallback will be used if VTP meshes are unavailable.
✅ Preview used C++ geometry (VTP meshes).

sphinxsim> preview --screenshot preview.png
🖼  Building configuration preview for: .../config.json
   Building C++ geometry; bounds cache fallback will be used if VTP meshes are unavailable.
✅ Preview used C++ geometry (VTP meshes).
📸 Screenshot saved to: preview.png

sphinxsim> preview --with-particles
🖼  Building configuration preview for: .../config.json
   Building C++ geometry; bounds cache fallback will be used if VTP meshes are unavailable.
   Particle generation overlay is enabled (--with-particles).
✅ Preview used C++ geometry (VTP meshes).

sphinxsim> continue-to-run --refresh-interval 10
✅ Simulation built
✅ Simulation initialized
🚀 Running simulation...
ℹ️ Preview checks for new snapshots every 10 seconds and plays each batch at up to 25 FPS.
✅ Simulation completed successfully!

For the full preview-and-animate workflow, load a JSON config and run:

sphinxsim> run --with-animation

This performs preview --with-particles followed by continue-to-run on the same generated simulation. Plain run remains unchanged. Once the animated run or a manual continue-to-run completes, enter replay to play its recorded particle snapshots again at up to 25 FPS:

sphinxsim> replay
▶️ Replaying 100 particle frames at up to 25 FPS.

If needed, replay opens the regular configuration preview, preserving the correct 2D/3D camera (including the orthographic XY view for 2D). Wait until continue-to-run has finished before starting replay. Replay keeps the current camera framing fixed while the particle snapshots animate.

preview requires a config to be loaded first (via load or generate).

After preview --with-particles, the shell retains the generated-particle SPHSimulation instance and its temporary runtime config for one immediate continue-to-run. This continues the same instance through buildSimulation(), initializeSimulation(), and run(), without generating particles again. Any other shell command discards the retained instance and its temporary config; use run when a fresh simulation from the saved config is intended.

continue-to-run accepts an optional wall-clock refresh interval:

sphinxsim> continue-to-run --refresh-interval 2.5

The default interval is 10 seconds and the value must be greater than zero. At each interval, the preview collects all available body-state VTP snapshots and plays them in sequence at up to 25 FPS. It then waits for another interval before collecting the next batch, allowing slower simulations to produce more output between playback batches. A snapshot is loaded only after its file size and modification time remain stable across checks, avoiding reads while the solver is still writing it. This uses pyvistaqt plus PySide6 or PyQt5; without a Qt-backed persistent preview, the simulation still continues but the window cannot refresh its particles live.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from sphinxsim.config.schemas import SimulationConfig
from sphinxsim.visualization.preview import ConfigVisualizer
import json

config_path = Path("my_config.json")
config = SimulationConfig(**json.loads(config_path.read_text()))

viz = ConfigVisualizer(config, project_root=Path("."), config_path=config_path)
viz.preview()                     # opens interactive window
viz.preview(title="My setup")     # custom window title
viz.preview(screenshot_path="preview.png")  # save screenshot, no window

docs.title: ConfigVisualizer parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description config SimulationConfig Validated Pydantic config object project_root Path Root of the SPHinXsim project (locates .build-temp/) config_path Path \| None Path to the original JSON file — passed directly to C++. Required for geometry rendering. off_screen bool Render off-screen when True (default False)

docs.title: preview() parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description title str "SPHinXsim - Configuration Preview" Window title with_particles bool False Run particle generation and overlay latest particles per body. In shell persistent mode, enabling this always redraws the scene. screenshot_path str \| Path \| None None When set, saves a screenshot to this path instead of opening a window. Implies off-screen rendering.

After rendering, the CLI reports which tier was used: - ✅ Preview used C++ geometry (VTP meshes). - ℹ️ Preview used C++ bounds fallback (no VTP meshes produced).

docs.title: Inspecting which tier was used
docs.text:
viz.preview()
print(viz.used_cpp_geometry)   # True if VTP meshes were rendered
print(viz.used_cpp_bounds)     # True if live C++ bounds were used

docs.title: VTP geometry (preferred)
docs.text:
The visualizer always:

  1. Passes your original JSON file directly to SPHSimulation (no copy written).
  2. Calls SPHSimulation.buildGeometries() from the C++ extension.
  3. The C++ builders write Shape<Name>.vtp files to .build-temp/preview_geometry/output/.
  4. PyVista reads and renders those polygon meshes.

This gives accurate geometry — including rotations, boolean-composition results, and imported triangle meshes.

docs.title: Bounds fallback
docs.text:
When VTP files are not produced, the visualizer queries getShapeBounds() from the geometry builder and renders axis-aligned bounding boxes from the cached shape bounds.

Both paths require the C++ extension. If geometry generation fails, or a shape has neither a readable VTP mesh nor cached bounds, the preview reports an error and does not show a partial/empty scene. If the extension is missing or incompatible, rebuild and reinstall the SPHinXsim Python binding as well as the C++ libraries.

docs.title: Shape types and VTP availability
docs.text:
Not all shape types produce VTP files in the C++ builders. Here is the complete mapping:

Shape type VTP written by C++? bounding_box ✅ Yes box (with transform/rotation) ✅ Yes expanded_box ✅ Yes multipolygon (2D) ✅ Yes triangle_mesh (3D) ✅ Yes complex_shape ❌ No (boolean composition of named sub-shapes)

complex_shape geometries are skipped in the VTP pass; their constituent sub-shapes are rendered individually via Tier 2 bounds.

docs.title: Annotations module
docs.text:
The sphinxsim.visualization.annotations module provides standalone label generators that can be used outside of PyVista:

from sphinxsim.visualization.annotations import body_label, oriented_box_label, gravity_label

# Human-readable body summary
label = body_label("WaterBody", config)
# → "Fluid: WaterBody\nρ=1000.0\nc=10.0"

# Oriented box with BC annotation
ob = config.geometries.oriented_boxes[0]
label = oriented_box_label(ob, config)
# → "Inlet [in_outlet]\nBC → WaterBody: emitter v=1.5"

# Gravity vector
g = gravity_label(config)
# → "g = (0.0, -9.81)"  or None if not set

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:
The visualization module is intentionally minimal for this phase. Planned extensions include:

  • SDF / level-set geometry: rendering signed-distance-function shapes once those are added to the geometry builder.
  • Initial condition colouring: colour-mapping particle regions by their initial temperature, velocity, or density.
  • BC arrow glyphs: directional arrows for inflow/outflow boundaries.
  • Embedded notebook support: inline rendering for Jupyter environments.

docs.title: SPHinXsim Workbench
docs.text: The desktop workbench places the PyVista Preview on the left and a shared sidebar on the right. JSON Editor and Chat are peer tabs in that sidebar, similar to switching assistants in VS Code. It uses the existing LLM provider configuration and AgentCAE worker, checkpoint and result interfaces.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
Use the Python environment containing the built SPHinXsim extensions and the chatbot and visualization extras (Chainlit, PySide6, PyVista and PyVistaQt):

python -m pip install -e '.[chatbot,visualization]'
$env:SPHINXSIM_LLM_PROVIDER = "mock"
python -m sphinxsim workbench

The mock provider needs no external API and is useful for checking the UI; natural-language chat requires a configured real provider. See LLM testing for provider configuration.

The default opens a workspace copy of the two-dimensional column-collapse demo; it does not edit the repository's demo file. To open your own JSON:

python -m sphinxsim workbench path/to/case.json --workspace .build-temp/workbench-demo

Existing workspace cases using container_box.inner_lower_bound and inner_upper_bound open with an updated inner_box in the editor draft. The JSON Editor tab marks this draft as unsaved. Review it and use Save + Preview to persist the updated geometry fields. Cases containing both representations or an incomplete pair of legacy bounds require an explicit edit.

Switch between JSON Editor and Chat using the right sidebar tabs. Both keep their state: switching preserves unsaved edits, editor selection and the chat conversation. Drag the vertical splitter to resize the sidebar. Preview remains visible at the full height of the left pane.

The JSON draft and left canvas are independent of the chat server. A local Chainlit child process is embedded in the Chat tab with Qt WebEngine. Startup errors are recorded in <workspace>/chat.log; use Reconnect chat to retry. The interface and embedded Chainlit controls use English.

The canvas reuses ConfigVisualizer, live VTP loading, and AgentPreviewObserver. VTK renders offscreen and Qt presents the frames, avoiding native OpenGL child window issues on Windows while retaining camera interaction. Drag to rotate, middle-drag to pan, use the wheel to zoom, and press R to reset the view. The left canvas contains the model and results; the Model Information sidebar is removed from the workbench, so the scene uses the full canvas width.

docs.title: Edit and preview
docs.text:
• JSON Editor uses the same Setting / Value property tree as the original shell Preview. Filter settings, expand or collapse groups, edit typed values, and add, duplicate, remove or reorder list entries. Revert undoes an edit; Reload reads the saved file after checking for unsaved changes. The shared formatter preserves existing field selection, numeric spelling, layout and LF/CRLF line endings, following upstream JSON Editor PRs #160 and #185.
  • Edit values, then Validate or Save + Preview (Ctrl+S). Invalid edits leave the saved file and last valid scene intact. Preview draft previews valid unsaved edits without saving them.
  • Initial particles enables particle generation for the next preview.
  • In chat, ask about the current JSON or send /config change end time to 0.08 seconds. The workbench and config_propose MCP tools produce a validated revision-bound proposal. In mock mode this example is deterministic; mock is not a natural-language model.
  • A new proposal marks the JSON Editor tab with a dot and leaves Chat visible. Switch to JSON Editor > LLM diff, click Apply proposal to draft, then Save + Preview. A star on JSON Editor indicates unsaved draft edits. Proposals cannot silently overwrite newer manual edits, and externally changed files must be reopened before saving.
  • Chat discovers the native MCP tools for configuration, CAD, job control, and result inspection. Send /mcp capabilities {} to inspect capabilities with a mock provider. Real LLM providers can select tools from the discovered schemas.
  • Run saved case starts an isolated C++ process using a snapshot of the saved configuration. Stop case run stops that manual run. Runtime logs and VTPs are kept below <workspace>/manual_runs/.

docs.title: Agent demonstration
docs.text:
Send the following in the embedded chat:

agent start Calibrate a 2D column-collapse runout extension to 0.2 m.
agent approve

Approval starts the existing durable worker, and the left canvas follows its VTP output without opening another Preview window. The Agent results selector switches between live, best, and completed candidates. Displayed run config is read-only; switching runs never overwrites the JSON draft.

Use agent status, agent report, agent cancel, or agent attach <workflow-id> followed by agent preview to reconnect. The desktop Attach control can also observe an existing workflow in the same workspace.

Agent start still generates an isolated calibration case from its plan; it does not automatically optimize the editor draft. Use Run saved case for the currently edited model. Only registered AgentCAE workflows are supported.

Closing the window stops its chat server and preview preparation. Durable Agent workers continue until completion or explicit agent cancel. Closing during a manual run requires confirmation and stops that run.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
$env:SPHINXSIM_LLM_PROVIDER = "mock"
python -m pytest tests/test_workbench.py tests/test_chainlit_chatbot.py tests/test_agent_preview.py -q -m "not integration"

Run the actual embedded browser, native Preview, short C++ simulation and Agent plan smoke test in a desktop session (mock LLM, no external API calls). It also checks visible Qt canvas pixels, mouse-wheel zoom, and native 3D preview with mouse-drag rotation:

$env:SPHINXSIM_RUN_WORKBENCH_DESKTOP = "1"
python -m pytest tests/test_workbench.py -q -k real_workbench_desktop

The desktop test saves screenshots and probe.json in its temporary workspace.

The workbench uses existing compiled modules; changing the desktop Python code does not require rebuilding C++.

docs.title: Simulating dambreak flows with SPHinXsim
docs.text:
This is the first example use to learn how to setting up a flow simulation using SPHinXsim. Note that, dambreak flow is a classical benchmark case for free-surface flow simulation using SPH method, and it has been widely used in the literature to validate the accuracy of SPH solvers.

The 2d and 3d dambreak examples demonstrate the basic usage of SPHinXsim for simulating free-surface flows. The canonical configurations are the 2d case and the 3d case.

Here, I show (2d) simulation setting json file to illustrate the basic usage.

docs.title: 2d dambreak simulation setting JSON file
docs.text:
{
  "characteristic_dimensions": [
    {
      "value": 1.0,
      "name": "Length",
      "hint": "geometries.shapes[name=WaterBody].upper_bound"
    },
    {
      "value": 1.0,
      "name": "Gravity",
      "hint": "gravity"
    },
    {
      "value": 1.0,
      "name": "Density",
      "hint": "fluid_bodies[name=WaterBody].material.density"
    }
  ],
  "simulation_type": "fluid_dynamics",
  "geometries": {
    "global_resolution": {
      "particle_spacing": 0.025
    },
    "shapes": [
      {
        "name": "WaterBody",
        "type": "bounding_box",
        "lower_bound": [0.0, 0.0],
        "upper_bound": [2.0, 1.0]
      },
      {
        "name": "WallBoundary",
        "type": "multipolygon",
        "polygons": [
          {
            "operation": "union",
            "type": "container_box",
            "inner_box": {
              "lower_bound": [0.0, 0.0],
              "upper_bound": [5.366, 5.366]
            },
            "thickness": 0.1
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  },
  "particle_generation": {
    "bodies": [
      {
        "name": "WaterBody"
      },
      {
        "name": "WallBoundary",
        "solid_body": {}
      }

    "relaxation_parameters": {
      "total_iterations": 1000
    }
  },
  "fluid_bodies": [
    {
      "name": "WaterBody",

        "density": 1.0
      }
    }

  "solid_bodies": [
    {

    {

    }

        }

    "output_interval": 0.1,
    "screen_interval": 100,

      "advection_cfl": 0.25,
      "particle_sort_frequency": 100
    }

}

docs.title: 1. Characteristic_dimensions
docs.text:
The characteristic_dimensions section defines scaling references for the simulation. If provided, it must include Length and at least one other characteristic dimension. In this example, Length, Gravity, and Density are provided.

Each entry requires a hint identifying the corresponding configuration value or stating that the reference is externally defined.

docs.title: 2. Simulation type
docs.text: The simulation_type field specifies the type of simulation being performed. In this case, it is set to "fluid_dynamics", indicating that the simulation is characterized by fluid flow, or the dynamics of the simulation is centered around the behavior of fluids. Other dynamics, such as solid dynamics, are considered as secondary dynamics in the simulation where the fluid-structure interaction is involved.

docs.title: 3. Geometries
docs.text:
This section defines the all geometries used in the simulation. Each geometry is defined by its type, name, and relevant parameters. The name of the geometry is used to reference it in other parts of the simulation settings, such as in the fluid_bodies, solid_bodies, and observers.

We first define the global_resolution for the simulation, which specifies the particle spacing used to discretize the geometries.

Then we define the main geometric components of the simulation, which include the shapes and the oriented_boxes. In dambreak case, we only define the shapes for the simulation, which include the WaterBody and the WallBoundary. We will learn more about the oriented_boxes in other cases.

As this is a 2d simulation, the WaterBody is defined as a bounding box with lower and upper bounds, while the WallBoundary is defined as a multipolygon. For multipolygon, the components are added one-by-one with a polygon and a binary operation. In this case, we define the WallBoundary as a union of a container box with inner lower and upper bounds and a thickness.

Note that for 3d simulations, the definition of the WaterBody and WallBoundary will be similar, but using 3d geometrical building blocks.

docs.title: 4. Particle generation
docs.text: particle_generation directly contains the bodies to generate and the relaxation_parameters. Each body name refers to a shape in geometries.shapes; include solid_body for a solid boundary. For a restart, set restart.restore_step to a saved step; particle generation and relaxation are skipped for nonzero restore_step.

docs.title: 5. Fluid bodies
docs.text: Here, we define the fluid bodies in the simulation. In this case, we have one fluid body named WaterBody, which is associated with a material of type weakly_compressible_fluid and a density of 1.0. Note that weakly_compressible_fluid is the default fluid type in SPHinXsim, and it is used to simulate incompressible fluids with a small compressibility.

docs.title: 6. Solid bodies
docs.text: Similarly, we define the solid bodies in the simulation. In this case, we have one solid body named WallBoundary, which is associated with a material of type rigid_body, which indicates that the body takes the role of wall boundary conditions.

docs.title: 7. Gravity
docs.text: Here, we define the gravity vector for the simulation. In this case, the gravity is set to an constant value of [0.0, -1.0].

docs.title: 8. Observers
docs.text: Observers are used to monitor specific variables at certain positions in the simulation domain. In this case, we have one observer named FluidObserver, which observes the WaterBody and records the Pressure variable at the position [5.366, 0.2]. The observer's data can be used for analysis and visualization of the simulation results.

docs.title: 9. Extra state recording
docs.text: Besides the observers, SPHinXsim also records state variables for all bodies. The extra_state_recording section specifies, beyond default variables setting, the extra variables to be recorded for each body. In this case, we record the Pressure variable for the WaterBody and the NormalDirection variable for the WallBoundary. Note that we need to specify the real_type or vector_type for the variables to be recorded.

docs.title: 10. Solver parameters
docs.text:
Here, we define the solver parameters for the simulation. The end_time field specifies the total simulation time, the output_interval field specifies the time interval for outputting simulation results, and the screen_interval field specifies the number of time steps between screen outputs. The fluid_dynamics field contains parameters specific to the fluid dynamics solver, including the acoustic_cfl, advection_cfl, and particle_sort_frequency values shown here. The acoustic_cfl and advection_cfl fields specify the CFL conditions for the acoustic and advection time steps, respectively. The particle_sort_frequency field specifies how often the particles are sorted to improve computational efficiency.

Note except for the end_time and output_interval have physical units and scaled by the characteristic dimensions defined in the characteristic_dimensions section, the other parameters are dimensionless.

docs.title: Notes on 3d dambreak simulation setting JSON file
docs.text:
The 3d dambreak simulation setting JSON file is similar to the 2d case, with the main difference being the definition of the geometries and the particle spacing. In the 3d case, the WaterBody is defined as a bounding box with lower and upper bounds in 3d space. The WallBoundary is a complex_shape formed by taking the union of an expanded box and subtracting the inner box. The particle spacing is also adjusted to account for the additional dimension, and the simulation parameters are scaled accordingly.

The 3d example also includes a cylindrical emitter shape. It is inserted into the fluid body's generated particles through particle_generation.bodies[].cylinder_shape_inserts. A matching region in geometries.oriented_boxes defines the emitter boundary condition's active region. The fluid_boundary_conditions entry uses type emitter, references that region by name, and sets inflow_speed and an optional on_schedule.

docs.title: Try to modify the JSON file for your own simulation
docs.text:
There are many parameters in the simulation setting JSON file that can be modified to create different simulation scenarios. For example, you can change the particle_spacing in the global_resolution section to adjust the resolution of the simulation, or modify the end_time and output_interval in the solver_parameters section to change the duration and frequency of the simulation output. You can also add or remove observers in the observers section to monitor different variables or positions in the simulation domain.

Another example is to modify the WaterBody geometry to change the initial shape of the fluid body, or adjust the WallBoundary geometry to create different boundary conditions for the simulation. You can also add solid bodies to the simulation by defining them in the solid_bodies section.

For 3d simulations, you can modify the geometries section to change the position and orientation of the emitter.

docs.title: Feedback and suggestions
docs.text: Please feel free to provide feedback and suggestions (in Issue of the SPHinXsim repository ) to improve the simulation setting JSON file and the documentation. Especially, if you feel something which may be confusing or unclear, please let us know so that we can make the necessary improvements.

docs.title: Simulating the filling tank flow with SPHinXsim
docs.text:
Compared to the dambreak flow, the filling tank flow is a more complex case, which involves a new boundary condition, i.e. emitter. Emitter is a boundary condition that can inject fluid particles into the simulation domain.

To facilitate emitter boundary condition, several JSON entries are added to the simulation setting file.

First, one need to define an oriented box as the geometry of the emitter, which is used to generate fluid particles. The geometry of the emitter can be defined in the geometries section of the JSON file, under the subsection oriented_boxes. The parameters of the oriented box are defined as shown below:

"geometries": {
    ...
    "oriented_boxes": [
      {
        "name": "Emitter",
        "type": "region",
        "half_size": [0.15, 0.0625],
        "transform": {
          "translation": [0.05, 1.0625],
          "rotation_angle": 0.0
        }
      }
    ]
}

The transform entry defines the position and orientation of the emitter region in the simulation domain. half_size gives its half-widths; together they define the region used to select particles for emission.

The fluid body's particle_reserve_factor reserves capacity for particles added by the emitter. It is a positive dimensionless capacity factor, not a count or a ratio describing the number of particles inside the emitter region:

"fluid_bodies": [
    {
      "name": "WaterBody",
      "material": {
        "type": "weakly_compressible_fluid",
        "density": 1.0
      },
      "particle_reserve_factor": 350.0
    }
  ]

The value shown is specific to this example. Choose a factor large enough for the expected particle growth during inflow.

Finally, one need to define the emitter boundary condition in the fluid_boundary_conditions section of the JSON file, as shown below:

"fluid_boundary_conditions": [
    {
      "body_name": "WaterBody",
      "oriented_box": "Emitter",
      "type": "emitter",
      "inflow_speed": 2.0,
      "on_schedule": {
        "switch_on_time": 1.0,
        "duration": 25.0
      }
    }
  ]

The inflow_speed entry defines the speed of the fluid particles injected into the simulation domain, and the optional on_schedule entry defines the time schedule for the emitter boundary condition. In this case, the emitter will be switched on at 1.0 and will last for 25.0.

docs.title: Simulating machine tooling with SPHinXsim
docs.text: In this tutorial, we will demonstrate how to simulate a milling process using SPHinXsim. The milling process involves the removal of material from a workpiece using a rotating cutting tool. This simulation will help us understand the dynamics of the cutting process and the interaction between the tool and the workpiece.

docs.title: Externally defined characteristic velocity
docs.text: Compared to previous tutorials, the characteristic dimension uses a different way to define the characteristic velocity. Here, the cutting speed is computed from the tool's angular velocity and diameter. Because the velocity is not represented by a single configuration field, its hint is externally_defined.

docs.title: Geometry of the milling tool
docs.text:
Another difference is that the we need read a data file for the geometry of the milling tool, which is defined in the geometries section of the JSON file, under the subsection shapes. The parameters of the mesh file are defined as shown below:

{
  "name": "MillingTool",
  "type": "multipolygon",
  "polygons": [
    {
      "operation": "union",
      "type": "data_file",
      "file_name": "milling_tool.dat"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Particle relaxation
docs.text:
Since the milling tool is a complex geometry, the example enables particle relaxation for it during particle generation, before the main simulation starts.

In the configuration, the milling tool's particle-generation body has "relaxation": {"level_set": {}}. This selects level-set relaxation for that body; the per-body setting is under particle_generation.bodies, while particle_generation.relaxation_parameters.total_iterations controls the iteration count.

The example sets total_iterations to 1000 in relaxation_parameters. This sets the number of relaxation iterations; it does not by itself guarantee that the particles are fully relaxed.

docs.title: Simulation type
docs.text: Milling simulation is not fluid simulation, so simulation_type is set to continuum_dynamics. In this example the deformable workpiece is the one continuum_body; the milling tool is a moving rigid solid_body. The J2 plasticity material and enabled ductile-damage model describe the workpiece's deformation and damage.

docs.title: Continuum bodies
docs.text:
Define the workpiece in continuum_bodies:

"continuum_bodies": [
    {
      "name": "ProcessingPiece",
      "material": {
        "type": "j2_plasticity",
        "density": 2.7,
        "sound_speed": 50.0,
        "youngs_modulus": 78.2e2,
        "poisson_ratio": 0.3,
        "yield_stress": 2.9e1,
        "hardening_modulus": 1.0,

        "ductile_damage": {
          "enabled": true,
          "threshold_equivalent_plastic_strain": 0.15,
          "critical_equivalent_plastic_strain": 0.5,
          "critical_damage": 1.0
        }
      }
    }
  ]

You will see that the material model used for the workpiece is j2_plasticity, which is a common material model for simulating plastic deformation in metals. The parameters of the material model, such as density, sound speed, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, yield stress, and hardening modulus, are defined in the material section of the JSON file.

There is also a ductile_damage entry, which indicates that the simulation will include a ductile damage model to simulate the failure and fracture of the workpiece during the milling process. The parameters of the ductile damage model, such as threshold equivalent plastic strain, critical equivalent plastic strain, and critical damage, are defined in the ductile_damage section of the JSON file.

docs.title: Moving the milling tool
docs.text: The milling tool and wall/container are the two rigid solid_bodies in this example. The tool is moving, as indicated by its is_moving entry.

docs.title: Body constraints
docs.text:
The prescribed movement of the milling tool and constraints on the working piece are defined in the body_constraints section of the JSON file. The parameters of the body constraints are defined as shown below:

  "body_constraints": [
    {
      "body_name": "MillingTool",
      "type": "simbody",
      "mobilized_body": "planar",
      "velocity": [0.0, -0.03],
      "angular_velocity": 2.0
    },

    {
      "body_name": "ProcessingPiece",
      "type": "fixed",
      "region": "ClampingRegion"
    }
  ]

Note that the milling tool is defined as a simbody type, which indicates that the rigid body dynamics of the milling tool will be simulated using the Simbody library. The mobilized_body entry is set to planar, which indicates that the milling tool will be constrained to move in a plane. The velocity and angular_velocity entries define the linear and angular velocities of the milling tool, respectively.

For the workpiece, the type entry is set to fixed, which indicates that the region entry is set to ClampingRegion, which indicates that the workpiece will be clamped in place using a specified region of the workpiece geometry.

The Simbody constraint also requires a top-level restart configuration. The complete working example, including that section and the geometry, is milling.json.

docs.title: Restarting the simulation
docs.text:
In this simulation, we will also demonstrate how to restart the simulation from a previous state. This can be useful for continuing a simulation that was interrupted or for running a simulation with different parameters starting from a previously computed state. Another usage is that one can use this approach to locate an issue (for example a blowup) which may occur during the simulation, by restarting the simulation from a previous state, one can check when, where and how this issue happens.

"restart": {
    "save_interval": 1000,
    "restore_step": 0,
    "summary_enabled": true
  }
You can see that the save_interval entry is set to 1000, which indicates that the simulation state will be saved every 1000 time steps. The restore_step entry is set to 0, which indicates that the simulation runs directly without restart. The summary_enabled entry is set to true, which indicates that a summary of the simulation state will be printed to the console when the restart file is written.

With non-zero restore_step, the simulation will be restarted from the specified time step, and the simulation state will be restored from the saved state at that time step. Note that, with restart, the particle generation will be disabled, which means that you should have valid simulation before (also restart file written at given restore_step). Otherwise, the simulation will not be able to run properly.
